items.prompt:
Read the fable.

A dog carrying a bone saw its reflection in a pond and thought it was another dog with a bigger bone. It snapped at the reflection and dropped its own bone into the water.

What is the lesson?
items.answer: The lesson is that being greedy can make you lose what you already have.

steps: The dog wanted the "bigger" bone in the reflection.
Snapping for it, it "dropped its own bone."
Greed cost the dog its bone.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Rosa was nervous to try out for the play, but she practiced her lines and went anyway. She got a part.

What lesson can we learn from Rosa?
items.answer: The lesson is that trying even when you are nervous can lead to good things.

steps: Rosa was "nervous" but "went anyway."
Because she tried, "she got a part."
Facing her fear paid off.

items.prompt:
Read the fable.

Ants asked a lazy grasshopper why he had no food in winter. "I sang all summer," he said. The ants had worked and now had plenty.

What central message does this fable share?
items.answer: The message is to work and prepare ahead of time instead of only playing.

steps: The grasshopper "sang all summer" and had nothing.
The ants "had worked" and had plenty.
Preparing ahead is the lesson.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Jamal kept interrupting his friends until no one wanted to talk to him. He noticed, started listening more, and his friends came back.

What is the lesson of this story?
items.answer: The lesson is that listening to others, instead of interrupting, keeps friends close.

steps: Interrupting drove his friends away.
When he "started listening more," they "came back."
Listening mended the friendships.

items.prompt:
Read the folktale.

A farmer's sons argued constantly. He gave each a single stick to snap, which they did easily. Then he tied ten sticks together, and no one could break the bundle.

What lesson is the farmer teaching?
items.answer: The lesson is that people are stronger together than alone.

steps: One stick snapped "easily."
Ten sticks tied together could not be broken.
The bundle stands for the sons; together they are strong.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Ella promised to feed the neighbor's cat while they were away. Some days she did not feel like it, but she went every single day. When the family returned, they trusted her with a summer job.

What message does this story teach?
items.answer: The message is that keeping your promises builds trust.

steps: Ella "went every single day," even when she did not feel like it.
Because she kept her promise, the family "trusted her with a summer job."
Reliability earned their trust.

items.prompt:
Read the fable.

A crow wanted to sing as sweetly as a nightingale, so it ignored its own strong flying and squawked all day, growing more and more unhappy.

What lesson does this fable share about being yourself?
items.answer: The lesson is to value your own strengths instead of wishing to be someone else.

steps: The crow ignored "its own strong flying" to copy the nightingale.
Trying to be someone else made it "unhappy."
It should value its own gifts.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

When a smaller kid dropped his lunch tray, some students laughed. Nadia knelt down, helped clean it up, and shared half her sandwich. The next week, others started helping too.

What central message does this story convey, and which detail shows it?
items.answer: The message is that one person's kindness can spread to others. The detail is that after Nadia helped, "others started helping too."

steps: Some students laughed, but Nadia "helped clean it up" and shared food.
Her example spread: "others started helping too."
Kindness can be contagious.

items.prompt:
Read the folktale.

A greedy man owned a goose that laid one golden egg each day. Wanting all the gold at once, he cut the goose open and found nothing inside. Now he had no eggs at all.

What lesson does this folktale teach, and how do the man's actions show it?
items.answer: The lesson is that greed can make you lose a good thing you already had. By cutting the goose open for all the gold at once, the man lost the daily golden egg entirely.

steps: The goose gave "one golden egg each day."
The man's greed made him "cut the goose open," finding "nothing."
His greed destroyed the steady gift.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Theo always waited until the night before to study and always felt panicked. After failing one quiz, he tried studying a little each night. His grades climbed, and tests stopped scaring him.

What is the central message, and which detail best proves it?
items.answer: The message is that steady effort over time works better than last-minute cramming. The detail that proves it is that once Theo studied "a little each night," his "grades climbed."

steps: Cramming left Theo "panicked" and failing.
Studying "a little each night" made his "grades climbed."
Steady effort was the fix.

items.prompt:
Read the myth.

A boy named Icarus flew with wax wings his father made. His father warned him not to fly too high, but Icarus soared toward the sun. The wax melted, and he fell into the sea.

What lesson does this myth teach about warnings?
items.answer: The lesson is to listen to wise warnings instead of letting pride push you too far.

steps: The father warned Icarus "not to fly too high."
Icarus ignored the warning and "soared toward the sun."
Ignoring good advice led to his fall.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

A new girl sat alone at lunch for a week. Everyone assumed she was unfriendly. When Maria finally sat with her, she learned the girl was just shy and had lots to say.

What central message does this story teach, and which detail supports it?
items.answer: The message is not to judge people before you get to know them. The supporting detail is that the 'unfriendly' girl was really "just shy and had lots to say."

steps: Everyone "assumed she was unfriendly."
In truth she was "just shy."
The assumption was wrong; do not judge too fast.

items.prompt:
Read the fable.

A mighty oak mocked the bending reeds in the marsh for being weak. When a great storm came, the reeds bent low and survived, but the stiff oak snapped and fell.

What lesson does the fable teach, and how do the oak and reeds show it?
items.answer: The lesson is that being flexible can help you survive better than being stiff and proud. The bending reeds "survived" the storm while the stiff oak "snapped and fell."

steps: The proud oak was "stiff"; the reeds could bend.
In the storm the reeds "survived" and the oak "snapped."
Flexibility beat stubborn strength.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Coach benched their star player, Ray, for skipping practice, even though it might cost the big game. Ray was angry at first, but he later thanked the coach, saying the rule finally taught him to show up for his team.

What is the central message, and which detail from the end best shows it?
items.answer: The message is that fair rules, even when they hurt, can help us grow. The detail that shows it is that Ray "later thanked the coach," saying the rule "taught him to show up for his team."

steps: The coach kept the rule even at a cost.
Ray was angry but "later thanked the coach."
The rule taught Ray responsibility.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

Zoe spent all recess perfecting her own poster and refused to help her group. Her poster was beautiful, but the group project fell apart and got a low grade, which counted for everyone, including Zoe.

State the central message in your own words and explain how Zoe's choice shows it.
items.answer: Message: putting yourself ahead of your team can end up hurting you too. Zoe's beautiful solo poster did not matter because the group project "fell apart and got a low grade" that counted for her as well.

steps: Zoe "refused to help her group" to perfect her own work.
The group project "fell apart" and the low grade "counted for everyone, including Zoe."
Her selfish choice hurt her in the end.
